$comment: THE LOWERING REGISTER — every CSS construct this pipeline LOWERS to a Figma construct, the context it fires in, what the inverse returns, and the canonical form the two directions must agree on. A DOOR (spec/door-register.json) decides whether a fact is ADMITTED; a LOWERING decides what SHAPE an admitted fact TAKES on the other surface. The forward direction had no register at all: core/emit-figma-script.ts is 8,230 lines and carries ZERO @door markers, and the door register's stage map has no `emit` entry — so every forward structure decision was unregistered and ungated. Held to the code by `npm run lowering:check`.

rules.ruleText: return 'stretch'; // 'normal' / 'stretch' — a grid item's default IS stretch

css.construct: justify-items / align-items / justify-self / align-self on a grid, with any value the mapper does not recognise
css.context: gridAlign maps center, start-family and end-family explicitly, and returns `stretch` for EVERYTHING else

figma.construct: stretch alignment, invented

lost: space-around, space-evenly, baseline and any unknown keyword — all collapse to stretch with no receipt
rules.canonical: stretch when CSS says stretch or normal; a named refusal otherwise
rules.why: The comment is right that `normal` means stretch for a grid item. The defect is the scope of the else: an unrecognised value is not the same as `normal`, and returning stretch for `baseline` invents an alignment the CSS never asked for. Adjacent to it, lowerTableDisplay hard-codes align:stretch for table and table-row from no observation at all — same pattern, same silence.

css.construct: a genuinely two-dimensional grid reaching the FLEX-LOWERING path
css.context: lowerGridDisplay, the fallback for inline-grid and for grids that declined structured promotion: more than one column AND more than one row

figma.construct: nothing — refused by name

lost: the whole layout for that container — named
rules.canonical: a named refusal: a 2D grid has no single-axis spelling
rules.why: A model refusal, and the reason the grid family is the healthiest in this register: lowering a 2D grid to a one-axis stack would require inventing an axis, so the code declines and says which grid and why. Nothing in the grid family drops silently — every impossibility is a throw or a named refusal.

css.construct: a second (or third) <svg> under a host element that already has an svg plan
css.context: the first svg found for a host wins; later ones are skipped

figma.construct: nothing for the later svgs — only the first becomes an icon

lost: every svg after the first per host — with receipt channel "none", fully silent
rules.canonical: one icon per host, chosen deliberately, with the others refused by name
rules.why: First-wins is a defensible tie-break; being silent about it is not. A button with a leading and a trailing icon is an ordinary shape, and this rule drops the second one without a word. It is one of the six structure decisions that carry receipt channel "none" — the silent frontier of the forward direction.

css.construct: the CSS emitted for a contract whose root carries no layout block
css.context: the code generator’s default for an absent root layout

figma.construct: n/a — this is the CSS the contract renders to

lost: the `flex` vs `inline-flex` distinction: the eliding side dropped `flex`, and this side restores `inline-flex`
rules.canonical: the two defaults must be the SAME keyword, or the elision is not an elision
rules.why: Reported as a defect of AGREEMENT rather than of either line alone. Neither default is wrong in isolation; together they guarantee that a root layout, once elided, comes back spelled differently. A contract that survives a round trip byte-for-byte is the property this whole exercise is for, and one keyword breaks it for every centered root.

css.construct: two or more adjacent inline siblings inside a block container — one CSS line box
css.context: computed to DECLINE the vertical rescue; the container then takes the horizontal default

figma.construct: nothing — the container falls through to a horizontal row

lost: the anonymous block / line-box structure, and the fact that it was declined at all — the comment above calls this "named residue" but no miss() or facts.push() ever fires
rules.canonical: a named refusal: an inline formatting context has no auto-layout spelling and should say so
rules.why: Reported as a receipt hole. The engine correctly identifies a construct it cannot express, and then says nothing — while the code comment claims it is named. A claim of honesty the code does not have is exactly what the door register was built to stop, and this site is outside its reach because emit has no doors.

css.construct: display:block carrying align/justify facts but no flex-direction
css.context: a layout exists, its direction is absent, and the declared display is exactly `block`

figma.construct: layoutMode VERTICAL with stretchChildren, alignment mapped from the carried align/justify

lost: counterAxisAlignItems BASELINE is silently coerced to MIN a few lines below, because Figma throws on BASELINE in a vertical stack
rules.canonical: a block-level box lowers to a vertical stack
rules.why: Right rule, too narrow a test. It matches `display === "block"` only, while the block-flow rescue thirty lines below was widened to block|list-item|flow-root|inline (the Carbon fix). So a `list-item` carrying layout.align still falls through to HORIZONTAL. The asymmetry between the two block branches is unreceipted and looks like an oversight rather than a decision.

css.construct: a block-flow container (block | list-item | flow-root | inline) with no layout fact
css.context: at least TWO in-flow children, and either all of them are block-level or some are and no two inline siblings are adjacent

figma.construct: layoutMode VERTICAL, MIN/MIN, stretchChildren

lost: a container with ONE child, or with a run of two adjacent inline children, never reaches this rescue and keeps the horizontal default
rules.canonical: a block-level box lowers to a vertical stack
rules.why: The best rule in the axis family: it reads CSS blockification properly rather than guessing, and a run of adjacent inline siblings really is one line box, so declining is correct there. The problem is what happens after it declines — the fall-through invents a row instead of refusing, and the decline itself is silent.

css.construct: any container whose flex-direction was not carried — including one that carries NO layout at all
css.context: the terminal fall-through of layoutSpec, after the block-flow rescues above have declined

figma.construct: layoutMode HORIZONTAL

lost: the distinction between "row was measured" and "nothing was measured" — both produce a row, and nothing receipts the second
rules.canonical: an explicit no-declared-axis outcome that refuses rather than defaults
rules.why: The candidate cause of "the dialog on one row", and the second half of a composition. Its partner is the fuse-side rule below: a non-flex container never receives a direction, so `l` arrives undefined here and the ternary supplies HORIZONTAL. Neither half is receipted, which is precisely why the symptom could never be cited to a line. The committed conformance case `display-block` already measures the outcome: seed `block`, and the value comes back as `flex`.

css.construct: display:block (or any block-flow display) on an icon part that also carries box channels
css.context: the icon-with-box host frame builds its layout inline and calls layoutSpec ONLY when resolveLayout returns something; otherwise it hard-codes a centered row

figma.construct: layoutMode HORIZONTAL, CENTER/CENTER — layoutSpec is never consulted

lost: every block-flow rescue in layoutSpec, for this whole class of part
rules.canonical: one axis rule for every part — the host frame must go through layoutSpec like everything else
rules.why: A bypass, not a decision: the blockification rescue was added to layoutSpec and these two construction sites were never routed through it. The text-with-box wrapper does the same thing a hundred and seventy lines later. Two code paths that build a frame without asking the function whose job is to decide a frame’s axis.

css.construct: a ROOT that carries no layout fact at all
css.context: layoutSpec, with no resolved layout and the root not declaring display:block

figma.construct: layoutMode HORIZONTAL, primaryAxisAlignItems CENTER, counterAxisAlignItems CENTER — an invented centered row

inverse.emits: no layout block at all (the proposal elides exactly this shape as "the generator default")
inverse.note: the two halves agree that row/center/center is the default — but packages/core/src/css.ts then re-inflates an absent root layout as INLINE-flex, so the display keyword flips on every trip

lost: the real CSS display of a layout-less root — it is not read, it is invented
rules.canonical: no layout invented: a root with no carried layout must lower to its declared display, and refuse rather than guess an axis
rules.why: The candidate cause of "cards as pills", cited to the line. A card-shaped contract whose root layout was never carried is drawn as a horizontally centered row — which IS the shape of a pill. There is no `layoutMode: 'NONE'` anywhere in this file (0 occurrences), so no frame is ever lowered to a non-auto-layout frame and this default is unavoidable once a root reaches here unclaimed. Stated as a candidate cause with the line cited, NOT as a verified fix — this PR changes no behaviour, so it cannot claim a symptom is closed.

css.construct: flex-direction: row-reverse / column-reverse
css.context: resolved per variant; the children array is reversed in place

figma.construct: the same children in reversed CHILD ORDER inside a forward auto-layout frame

inverse.emits: a plain forward stack — the reverse-ness is not a canvas fact and cannot be read back
inverse.note: the render is right and the fact is gone; a second forward pass over the returned contract would NOT re-reverse, so the render is stable but the authored spelling is not

lost: `row-reverse` / `column-reverse` as a declared fact — only its effect on order survives
rules.canonical: reversed child order, with the reverse keyword refused by name
rules.why: Genuinely the right lowering — Figma has no reverse flag, and reversing the children produces the identical render. It belongs in the register because the loss is real and unnamed, and because the schema disagrees with itself about it: LayoutSchema.direction admits only row|column, while the proposal appends `-reverse` to that same field and only VariantLayoutSchema accepts it.

rules.ruleText: const l = spec.layout || { mode: 'HORIZONTAL', primary: 'MIN', counter: 'MIN' };${hasGrid ? `
rules.markerOutsideRule: the deciding line is inside the serialized in-page plugin runtime (a template literal), which is emitted as the generated Figma script rather than executed here — a `//` line there would become generated text, not a source marker, so this rule is pinned by its rule text instead

css.construct: any node reaching the generated plugin runtime with no compiled layout
css.context: applyFrameSpec, the last backstop — by construction nothing upstream claimed this node

figma.construct: layoutMode HORIZONTAL, MIN/MIN

lost: the third and last chance to notice that no axis was ever measured
rules.canonical: no layout invented at the backstop — a node that reaches the runtime unclaimed is a defect upstream and should be named, not defaulted
rules.why: The third of three independent places that turn "unknown" into "row" (the other two are the layout-less root default and the terminal ternary). Three defaults, one direction, no receipts — which is why a horizontal-row symptom has three possible origins and no way to tell them apart from the output.

rules.ruleText: layout: resolveLayout(part, subst) ? layoutSpec(part, false, subst) : { mode: 'HORIZONTAL', primary: 'MIN', counter: 'MIN' },

css.construct: a text part carrying a padding channel, whose display is block-flow
css.context: wrapTextInBox builds the wrapper; with no resolved layout it takes a hard-coded MIN/MIN row rather than asking layoutSpec

figma.construct: layoutMode HORIZONTAL, MIN/MIN

lost: the block-flow rescue, for every padded text box
rules.canonical: one axis rule for every part
rules.why: The twin of the icon-host bypass, and the reason the axis family needs a register: the same decision is taken in four different places in one file, three of them defaulting to a row, and no two of them agree about which inputs matter.

css.construct: a LITERAL column-gap on a VERTICAL stack (and the row-gap twin four lines below)
css.context: litPx already returned a number, so its own literalMiss did not fire; the condition is simply false and there is no else

figma.construct: nothing

lost: the cross-axis gap, with NO receipt of any kind — no miss(), no literalMiss(), no fact
rules.canonical: a named refusal, exactly as the token path already does
rules.why: Reported as a BUG, not a decision. The token path for the identical situation calls miss() and says why; the literal path drops the value with an `if` that has no else. Same construct, same impossibility, half of it named and half silent — nobody chose that. The fix is one else branch, and it is not made here.

rules.ruleText: miss(spec, cssProp, 'the cross axis of a VERTICAL stack — Figma has one itemSpacing and it is the main axis.', ref);

css.construct: column-gap bound to a token on a VERTICAL stack (and, at the twin site, row-gap on a HORIZONTAL one)
css.context: the gap names the CROSS axis, which Figma has no field for

figma.construct: nothing — refused

lost: the cross-axis gap — named
rules.canonical: a named refusal

receipt.marker: the cross axis of a VERTICAL stack

rules.why: The right answer, receipted. Figma has exactly one itemSpacing and `counterAxisSpacing` is never written anywhere in this file (0 occurrences), so a cross-axis gap genuinely has nowhere to go. This rule is the standard its literal twin below fails to meet.

css.construct: column-gap bound to a token
css.context: the part’s layout mode is HORIZONTAL, so column-gap is the MAIN axis

figma.construct: bindings.itemSpacing, bound to the same variable

inverse.note: the axis-specific spelling is lost: column-gap goes out and the generic `gap` comes back

lost: the axis-specific spelling — the conformance baseline records this verbatim as "channel respelled: column-gap → gap"
rules.canonical: gap on the parent
rules.why: Correct and measured — `flex-gap` round-trips today. The respelling is a genuine asymmetry rather than a defect: Figma has ONE itemSpacing and it is the main axis, so on a horizontal row `column-gap` and `gap` are the same fact, and `gap` is the form that survives the trip. Naming it here is what stops it being read as drift.

css.construct: row-gap and column-gap on a grid container
css.context: grid keeps BOTH axes — unlike flex, where one itemSpacing forces a choice

figma.construct: rowGap and columnGap on the GRID frame, independently

inverse.note: an authored `gap` shorthand and an authored row-gap/column-gap pair are indistinguishable in CSSOM, so the pair is the only recoverable form

lost: the authored `gap` shorthand spelling — receipted by name in the anatomy stage
rules.canonical: the independent { row, column } pair
rules.why: Both gap cases round-trip, and this is the rule that proves the flex side did not have to be lossy. The SAME CSS construct gets two different answers depending on the parent’s display: grid carries the pair, flex cannot spell row-gap at all. One of those two answers is a limitation of Figma; the other is a limitation of the schema, and the register is where that distinction becomes visible.

rules.ruleText: const trackWrite = (t) => (t.type === 'HUG' ? { type: 'HUG' } : { type: t.type, value: t.value });
rules.markerOutsideRule: the deciding line is inside the serialized in-page plugin runtime (a template literal), which is emitted as the generated Figma script rather than executed here — a `//` line there would become generated text, not a source marker, so this rule is pinned by its rule text instead

css.construct: a fit-content grid track
css.context: runtime track write — a HUG track must be written as the bare type with NO value

figma.construct: { type: 'HUG' }, never { type: 'HUG', value: n }

lost: nothing — the asymmetry is in the API and the rule accommodates it
rules.canonical: fit-content lowers to a bare HUG track
rules.why: Registered because it is a lowering rule that exists ONLY because of an API asymmetry, and it is exactly the kind of thing that gets silently undone by a well-meaning refactor. The Figma API reads a HUG track back with a value attached, and writing that value back reinterprets the track as FIXED at that number — every fit-content track silently became a 1px column. The rule is right, it is named, and now it is gated.

css.construct: grid-template-columns / grid-template-rows
css.context: a carried structured grid; each track lowers by kind — px to FIXED, fr to FLEX, fit-content to HUG

figma.construct: layoutMode 'GRID' with FIXED / FLEX / HUG tracks, plus gridRowCount and gridColumnCount

inverse.emits: grid-template-columns / grid-template-rows in the declared spelling

lost: minmax(), repeat(), named lines and auto-fit/auto-fill have no spelling and are refused upstream by the grid fences
rules.canonical: grid-template-columns / grid-template-rows in the declared spelling
rules.why: Worth stating plainly: the schema comment says "Figma has no grid track sizing; the canvas lowers grids to nested auto-layout stacks", and that prose is now OUT OF DATE. Figma shipped a native GRID layout mode with FIXED/FLEX/HUG tracks, this emitter uses it, and four track cases round-trip. The register records the rule the engine actually implements, which is better than the one the schema still describes.

css.construct: margin: auto — the standard "push to the far edge" and "centre in the container" idiom
css.context: parseLitPx accepts only a signed decimal with an optional px/rem/em unit. `auto` fails the regex and returns undefined; the token path additionally requires a finite number.

figma.construct: nothing — it is never lowered to SPACE_BETWEEN, to MAX counter-axis alignment, or to a spacer

lost: the auto margin, in both directions
worse: Chromium resolves `auto` to its USED px value, so fusion can mint a harness-stage-derived number as a design token — the viewport-geometry defect class, with no equivalent door
rules.canonical: a named refusal — `auto` margins must be REFUSED by name, never lowered to a used pixel value
rules.why: Registered as a WALL rather than a proposal because the honest answer is refusal, not lowering. `justify-content: space-between` is a real Figma fact and `margin-left: auto` sometimes means it, but only sometimes — and the difference is not recoverable from a used pixel value. This tree already has a doctrine for numbers that are functions of the capture window (fuse.viewport-derived-geometry-refused): refuse them by name. `auto` margins have no such door, and that is the gap.

rules.markerOutsideRule: the deciding line is inside the serialized in-page plugin runtime (a template literal), which is emitted as the generated Figma script rather than executed here — a `//` line there would become generated text, not a source marker, so this rule is pinned by its rule text instead

css.construct: margin-* on a direct child of a STANDALONE component’s root, amended rather than created
css.context: amendComponent emits insetOverlayCall, gridChildrenCall, outOfFlowResizeCall and birthBoxCall on this line — but NOT marginBoxCall. The two paths that do call it are buildNode (create) and amendSet.

figma.construct: nothing — no margin box is built on this path

lost: every residual margin on a standalone component’s direct children, on the amend path only
and it is not even named: refuseSkippedMargins covers FILL/grow/out-of-flow/empty, not this exit
rules.canonical: the same lowering the create path performs — create and amend must agree
rules.why: Reported as a plain BUG, not a decision. Three call sites exist for birthBoxCall (buildNode, amendSet, amendComponent) and only two for marginBoxCall — the third was missed. Nothing in the code or the register says amend should differ from create here, and a fact that survives creation but vanishes on re-sync is the shape of defect this tree keeps finding. Not fixed in this PR: a fix shipped inside a documentation PR is how unexercised claims get made.

css.construct: margin-* on a child the margin box provably cannot wrap
css.context: refuseSkippedMargins, running AFTER annotateFillW: the child is out of flow, or carries grow, or fillW, or is an empty runtime-sized frame (frame, 0 children, no fixedHeight/lits.height/shape)

figma.construct: nothing — the margins are stripped from the spec before the runtime sees them

lost: the margin, entirely — but named, with the side list and the reason
rules.canonical: a named refusal (FC-EMIT-MARGIN-BOX-SKIPPED)
rules.why: One of the honest rules in this file, and the model the rest of the margin family should follow: it computes exactly why the wrapper cannot be built, refuses, and says so by name in a code the conformance baseline can quote. A FILL-sized child genuinely cannot be wrapped without destroying the fill, so refusing beats inventing.

rules.markerOutsideRule: the deciding line is inside the serialized in-page plugin runtime (a template literal), which is emitted as the generated Figma script rather than executed here — a `//` line there would become generated text, not a source marker, so this rule is pinned by its rule text instead

css.construct: residual margin-* on an in-flow child that no gap or padding lowering consumed
css.context: runtime: the child is not overlay/insetOverlay/absolute/grow, and NEITHER axis reads layoutSizingHorizontal/Vertical === FILL

figma.construct: a synthetic FRAME named "<child> (margin box)", fills [], clipsContent false, sized w+l+r × h+t+b, child placed at (l, t)

inverse.emits: an ordinary anatomy part — the wrapper is read back as a real FRAME part of the component
inverse.note: THE fixed-point violation. `grep -a "(margin box)"` over the 11,574-line inverse returns exactly ONE hit, at propose-figma.ts:3850, and it is a mention inside a note string — not a recognizer. The inverse cannot see its own forward artifact.

lost: the margin itself, as a margin — it becomes wrapper geometry
the fixed point: pass 1 mints the wrapper, the inverse promotes it to a real part, pass 2 lowers THAT part again, so the structure grows every pass
rules.canonical: gap or padding on the parent, with any residual REFUSED by name — never a synthetic node
rules.why: This is the incumbent, and it is the thing that already broke. It is option (a) — the spacer node — with the inverse half never written, and its measured result is the committed NAMED failure on the one margin case the kit has, plus unbounded structure growth across passes. The register records it as implemented because it IS what the engine does, and names the canonical form it does not reach.

css.construct: adjoining vertical margins between block-flow siblings (margin-bottom of one, margin-top of the next)
css.context: lowerMarginGaps computing the inter-sibling gap. The sum t + l is CORRECT on a HORIZONTAL row — horizontal margins do not collapse. It is WRONG on a VERTICAL stack, where CSS block flow collapses adjoining margins to max(t, l).

figma.construct: itemSpacing = t + l

inverse.note: the inverse emits `gap`, and `gap` does NOT collapse — so the doubled value is re-authored as a real doubled gap and the error is laundered into the contract

lost: the collapsed value: margin-bottom:16 + margin-top:16 renders as 16px in CSS and is lowered as itemSpacing: 32
rules.canonical: gap on the parent, equal to the COLLAPSED value
rules.why: Not a style preference — a measurable defect with no receipt. `grep -rn "collaps"` across /core finds only stroke-glyph collapsing; nothing in the forward path models block-flow margin collapsing. The rule must resolve to the collapsed value BEFORE lowering, and the axis is the discriminator: keep the sum for HORIZONTAL, take max() for VERTICAL. Load-bearing for the fixed point too — only the collapsed gap converges, because the inverse re-emits `gap`, which never collapses.

css.construct: margin-* lowered to itemSpacing whose contributing margins name more than one token, or none
css.context: the uniform-gap lowering succeeded, but the margins do not all resolve to ONE token variable (sources.size !== 1, or any contributor is a bare literal)

figma.construct: a LITERAL itemSpacing (spec.lits.itemSpacing), not a bound variable

inverse.emits: gap on the parent as a literal px value
inverse.note: a literal cannot name the token it came from, so the return trip cannot restore the binding

lost: the token identity of the gap — the Figma inspector shows a number where the library authored a spacing token
rules.canonical: gap on the parent, bound to the token when one token explains every contributor
rules.why: Defensible as far as it goes: Figma binds ONE variable to itemSpacing, so two different tokens genuinely cannot both be carried, and a literal preserves the render. What is not defensible is the silence — losing a token binding is exactly the kind of fact this tree receipts everywhere else, and here nothing is said at all.

css.construct: margin-* on the ONLY in-flow child of a container
css.context: lowerMarginGaps declines here: with fewer than two children there is no inter-sibling gap to compute, so a lone child’s margin is never lowered to any parent field. It falls through to the (margin box) wrapper instead.

figma.construct: nothing — the margin survives on the child and is later drawn as a synthetic wrapper frame

lost: the chance to express the space as parent padding, which is what it renders as
the child’s ability to respond to parent resize, because the wrapper it takes instead is FIXED-sized
rules.canonical: padding-* on the parent, on the matching sides
rules.why: Space between a lone child and its container edge is indistinguishable, in the rendered box, from container padding — and Figma has padding but not margin. The guard the rule needs: the container must carry no competing declared padding on that side, or the two sum. Today this case takes the wrapper, which is strictly worse: a FIXED frame that stops the child reflowing, and an artifact the inverse cannot recognise.

css.construct: margin-* between in-flow siblings, on the parent’s MAIN axis
css.context: lowerMarginGaps: the parent carries a layout, no CSS `gap` already claimed itemSpacing, ≥2 in-flow children (no overlay/insetOverlay/absolute), and every inter-sibling trail(i)+lead(i+1) sum is EQUAL and > 0

figma.construct: itemSpacing on the parent auto-layout frame
figma.note: the consumed margins are then deleted from the children, so the fact exists once, on the parent

inverse.note: the inverse cannot know the canvas gap was authored as sibling margins; it emits `gap`, which is the CSS the author should have written

lost: which of the two siblings owned the space (CSS margin is per-child; Figma itemSpacing is per-parent)
the distinction between `gap: 16` and `margin-bottom: 16` on every child but the last
rules.canonical: gap on the parent
rules.why: This is the owner’s own rule, already the engine’s behaviour, never written down or defended. Figma’s itemSpacing IS between-sibling space — the only construct in the API with the same meaning. The asymmetry is admitted rather than hidden: the round trip converges on `gap`, and `gap` is the canonical form because it is the one spelling both surfaces can hold. The all-or-nothing uniformity guard is right: a non-uniform run has no single itemSpacing, and inventing one would change the render.

css.construct: padding-left / -right / -top / -bottom bound to a token
css.context: each side independently bindable; the logical padding-inline / padding-block forms bind the same variable to both sides

figma.construct: bindings.paddingLeft (and siblings) bound to the same variable

inverse.site: padding-* proposed from the bound padding fields
inverse.emits: padding-inline / padding-block when both sides share a variable, padding-* longhands otherwise
inverse.note: the baseline records this verbatim as "channel respelled: padding-left → padding-inline"

lost: the authored spelling: a longhand pair with one token returns as the logical shorthand
rules.canonical: the logical shorthand when both sides agree, longhands otherwise
rules.why: The cleanest lowering in the file, and the one to hold the others to: Figma has four padding fields, CSS has four padding longhands, and they mean the same thing. Both padding conformance cases round-trip. The respelling is named here so it is never mistaken for drift.

rules.ruleText: if (reg && reg.canvas !== 'draw') miss(spec, cssProp, reg.note, ref);

css.construct: any token-bound channel with no case in the switch — including the `padding` shorthand itself
css.context: the token default branch receipts ONLY when the channel exists in TOKEN_CHANNELS and is marked non-draw; a channel absent from that registry falls through with nothing

figma.construct: nothing

lost: the value, AND the receipt, for any channel the registry does not carry — the receipt is conditional on the very registry that failed to know about the channel
rules.canonical: a named refusal for every unhandled channel, whether or not a registry row exists
rules.why: A receipt guarded by the wrong condition. The literal side of the same switch calls literalMiss() in ALL branches including the catch-all else, and has no such hole. This matters beyond padding: it is the general escape through which any unregistered token channel leaves without a word, which is the shape of the tab-size incident that once made validateContract refuse 32 whole components.

rules.markerOutsideRule: the deciding line is inside the serialized in-page plugin runtime (a template literal), which is emitted as the generated Figma script rather than executed here — a `//` line there would become generated text, not a source marker, so this rule is pinned by its rule text instead

css.construct: n/a — canvas placement has no CSS source; this is a pure forward-only structure decision
css.context: ensureHostSection, run unconditionally after the create block, from all three call sites: the create path, amendSet and amendComponent

figma.construct: the host section is moved to (100, 100) on its page

lost: the designer’s own positioning of the host section — silently reverted on every amend
rules.canonical: position on create; never move an existing section on amend
rules.why: ensureHostSection runs this write UNCONDITIONALLY, after the create block, so it fires whether the section was just created or found by its existing marker — and it is reached from all three call sites: the create path and both amend paths. Every component this emitter touches is pinned to the same coordinate, which is also why several sets can end up stacked at one point. Registered as a decision because placement genuinely is one; registered as `proposed` because reverting a human’s deliberate edit, with no receipt, cannot be the intended one.

rules.markerOutsideRule: the deciding line is inside the serialized in-page plugin runtime (a template literal), which is emitted as the generated Figma script rather than executed here — a `//` line there would become generated text, not a source marker, so this rule is pinned by its rule text instead

css.construct: n/a — the arrangement of variant cells within a component set
css.context: the per-variant placement loop, on both the create and the amend path, from accumulated column and row extents plus a fixed pad

figma.construct: each variant cell placed on a padded grid derived from accumulated column and row extents

lost: nothing meaningful — variant cell coordinates are presentation, not contract
rules.canonical: variant cells laid out on a deterministic grid
rules.why: Registered as a deliberate, defensible forward-only decision, to make the point that not every unregistered rule is a defect. Cell coordinates carry no library fact, the layout is deterministic, and the inverse correctly ignores it. Its neighbour twenty lines away — the pinned section origin — looks identical in shape and is not defensible, and the only way to tell them apart is to write both down.

css.construct: position:absolute with all four insets carried and every one a px length
